listenings.text: I've been a family doctor for twenty years, and the most important thing I've learned is that the first question is rarely the real one. A patient comes in and asks about a pain in her knee. We talk about the knee for ten minutes. Then, with her hand on the door handle, she says, 'Oh, and one more thing.' And that one more thing is the reason she came. So now I ask follow-up questions early. I don't ask, 'Is that all?', because people always say yes. I ask, 'What else is worrying you today?' It's an open-ended question, and it gives people permission to talk. I also ask, 'Who sent you here?' or 'What made you call this week, and not last month?' Something happened this week. Someone said something. When I find out what it was, the visit takes the same time, but it's a completely different visit. My patients don't hide things from me on purpose. They're just waiting for the right question.

I've interviewed politicians on the radio for twenty-five years, and young reporters always ask me the same thing: how do you prepare your questions? The truth is that I prepare only the first one. The interview happens in the second question. A politician answers the first question with a speech he has practiced at home. My job is to listen for the one word that doesn't fit. If he says, 'Mistakes were made,' I ask, 'Who made them?' If he says, 'We spoke to the community,' I ask, 'Who did you speak to? And when?' Short questions work best, because long questions give people time to escape. And I never ask two questions at once, because people always answer the easy one. One more thing: silence. When an answer stops too early, I don't say anything for three seconds. Very often, the most interesting sentence of the whole interview comes right after that silence.
